messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] CHANGE FROM GEOGRAPHICAL COORDINATES TO UTM COORDINATES IN AN INLA INTERPOLATION PERFORMED IN R
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The geom_sf() method from ggplot draws the data in the coordinate system the data is stored in (such as utm), but adds longitude/latitude markings to the plot. So even though it looks like it draws in long/lat, that’s not actually the case.

Unfortunately I haven’t figured out if there’s an option to _not_ do that, and instead show the local coordinate system coordinates. I think the easiest approach is to manually set the CRS info to NA just for plotting; it should then show the actual coordinates.

st_crs(prediction_points_clipped) <- st_crs(NA)

perhaps?

Finn

messages.subject: The range hyperparameter in SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I understand it is impossible to know the range in the SPDE before modeling, however, is there a rule of thumb or something else to help you guess the initial range and sigma hyperparameters before modeling?

Thanks.

```
# The SPDE Model
nu <- 1 # Matern smoothness parameter
alpha <- 2
r0 <- 20
#Matern SPDE model object using inla.pcmatern
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
                            alpha = alpha,
                            prior.range = c(r0, 0.01),
                            prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01))
```

However, the code you provided is to set the parameters for the PC-priors on these hyperparameters. This is something else and can affect the results.

Elias.

prior distributions for the range and sigma (standard deviation). But
that's not the same as setting initial values for optimisation. it's
not clear if you're asking about priors, initial values, or both.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Variability explained
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

this question has multiple potential answers, depending on the reason
for asking it, and no one true correct answer. For instance, since the
spatial field component has posterior correlation with the "fixed
effects", the variation contribution of each individual effect can add
up to more than the combined variability, so computing a "percentage
of explained variance" doesn't necessarily mean what one thinks it
means.

But you may be on the right track in thinking about what happens to
the model when removing one model components, and comparing the
results. We did something along those lines in
Yuan Yuan, Fabian E. Bachl, Finn Lindgren, David L. Borchers, Janine
B. Illian, Stephen T. Buckland, Håvard Rue, and Tim Gerrodette (2017),
"Point process models for spatio-temporal distance sampling data from
a large-scale survey of blue whales", Annals of Applied Statistics,
11, 2270--2297, doi:10.1214/17-AOAS1078
There, we compared the spatial model predictions with and without the
random field component present in the estimation, and computed the
overall spatial variability (in the spatial context, overall spatial
variability is arguably the relevant quantity, and not raw statistical
variance at the observation locations).
What you describe sounds similar, but with looking only at the
locations where you have observations.
Both versions require you to run the model twice; one with the f(s,
...) component, and once without it.  There's no special magic to
this.

Note:
Due to the posterior dependence, I prefer looking at the combined
component effects when comparing models; i.e. I would mainly compare
combined predictor values, and not the individual component estimates,
as those have different interpretation in the presence of other model
components (spatial confounding is virtually ubiquitous, and one
should not expect "spatial fixed effect" estimates to remain unchanged
when adding other spatial components to the model).

Finn

Hi Finn, thank you for your answer. I read the paper you mentioned and I think that I get what you mentioned.
Reading the paper in some part you did this

So I gues that I should do what you mentioned, run the model the first time with the spatial effect and see which ones do not have the 0 in the posterior credible interval and then a second time without the spatial effect and see which ones have the 0 and see how in the presence of f(s, model = spde) some variables can or cannot explain the spatial effect?

And to compute the overall spatial variability I think that with INLA one can do that using this:

mod.field = inla.spde2.result(res, name="s", spde)
mod.field$summary.hyperpar

So I get theta1 and theta2 and their mean, sd, an posterior credible interval, then if theta2 (I guess that is sigma and theta1 is the range) is significant their mean would be the overall spatial variability?

And lastly, one question that appeared while reading this, I can use the significance of the variables to see how this changes with and without spatial effect as mentioned above, but even if the variable is non significant that is not enough reason to remove the variable, even in the presence of a spatial effect, right? I am asking this because I did a model selection using the DIC criteria but when I see the significance to see how much of the spatial effect is explained by them, one of my two covariables are not significant so that covariable cannot explain the log-spatial effect (I have a lognormal model) but the predictions are better with this term (and I am mostly interested only on those predictions), but in the paper you mentioned, because of that significance you are going to remove the variables, so what should be the correct procedure here?

Thank you!!

On Monday, June 3, 2024 at 9:01:09 AM UTC-5 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi,
>
> this question has multiple potential answers, depending on the reason
> for asking it, and no one true correct answer. For instance, since the
> spatial field component has posterior correlation with the "fixed
> effects", the variation contribution of each individual effect can add
> up to more than the combined variability, so computing a "percentage
> of explained variance" doesn't necessarily mean what one thinks it
> means.
>
> But you may be on the right track in thinking about what happens to
> the model when removing one model components, and comparing the
> results. We did something along those lines in
> Yuan Yuan, Fabian E. Bachl, Finn Lindgren, David L. Borchers, Janine
> B. Illian, Stephen T. Buckland, Håvard Rue, and Tim Gerrodette (2017),
> "Point process models for spatio-temporal distance sampling data from
> a large-scale survey of blue whales", Annals of Applied Statistics,
> 11, 2270--2297, doi:10.1214/17-AOAS1078
> There, we compared the spatial model predictions with and without the
> random field component present in the estimation, and computed the
> overall spatial variability (in the spatial context, overall spatial
> variability is arguably the relevant quantity, and not raw statistical
> variance at the observation locations).
> What you describe sounds similar, but with looking only at the
> locations where you have observations.
> Both versions require you to run the model twice; one with the f(s,
> ...) component, and once without it. There's no special magic to
> this.
>
> Note:
> Due to the posterior dependence, I prefer looking at the combined
> component effects when comparing models; i.e. I would mainly compare
> combined predictor values, and not the individual component estimates,
> as those have different interpretation in the presence of other model
> components (spatial confounding is virtually ubiquitous, and one
> should not expect "spatial fixed effect" estimates to remain unchanged
> when adding other spatial components to the model).
>
> Finn
>
> On Mon, 3 Jun 2024 at 03:26, Richard <richard...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear INLA team
> >
> > I have created a spatial model and I am interested to see how much of the variability is explained by each term, especially by the spatial effect, is there any way to do this? Let´s say I have this model:
> >
> > y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + f(s, model = spde)
> >
> > Is there any way to check how much each terms help to explain the variability?
> >
> > One thing I did, but I am not sure if there is a better option, and it is just graphical, is to see how well the posterior follows the sample, so I use inla.posterior.sample and get the first n-predictors that correspond to the sample of size n, the idea is that those predictors are similar to the observed data.
> >
> > I am not sure if by removing each of terms once and see how much the posterior changes compared to the data could help to show how much each term helps to compute the posterior but is not exactly an explanation of the variability and I am more interested in something numeric rather than graphic.
> >
> > Is there any way to do this?
> >
> > Thank you
> >

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Variability explained
messages.body_plain:
Theta1 and theta2 are the internal parameterisation of the “humanly interpretable” parameter. The spde2.result function converts them into humanly interpretable format. But when using pcmatern models, already the $summary.hyperpar output is in humanly interpretable scale (range and sigma).

However, when I said spatial variability I meant just that, and _not_ the model _parameter_ sigma. The distinction is subtle, and if one had a iid model component they would be almost the same as each other. But in the presence of strong spatial correlation, the actual variability within the domain can be _smaller_ than the model parameter value.
I’m referring to the difference between
  Var(u(s)|Y) = sigma^2,
which  is the posterior  variance of the random field u(.), and
  V(D) = \frac{1}{|D|} \int_D [u(s) - M(D)]^2 ds,
where
  M(D) = \frac{1}{|D|} \int u(s) ds

The posterior expectation of V(D) is the “posterior expected mean square deviation from the spatial average”, and this is more directly measuring the amount of spatial variability in u(s) than \sigma^2.

That said, people tend to ignore that and just talk about sigma anyway…

“Statistical insignificance” of a variable is usually not a reason to remove it from the model; I would only remove it if keeping it in the model causes numerical problems or excessive runtime. But this is a large complicated philosophical issue that one can spend weeks on in a modern class on statistical modelling…

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

having the covariate evaluator function call fill_missing() is the likely issue with runtime for predictions, in case that means it tries to evaluate it for all those locations outside the grid. But 40x40 should be ok even for that.
But to be safe, you might need to make the covariate field complete before calling the inlabru methods, so it only needs to do that _once_, and not every time you evaluate the predictor.
But with just 1 sample and 40x40 I wouldn't expect it to take that long.

Can you consider changing from sp to sf? I'm reluctant to spend time on debugging sp specific code anymore; if sf/terra works, it would be better.
(Most of the online inlabru examples have been converted to sf/terra, although we don't seem to have a good example for how to do fill_missing in combination with terra rasters; the principle is the same as for sp, but the code details are slightly different I think).

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I wanted to enquire which rule should one use when setting the priors for the range and sigma in the SPDE. I have noted changing these values (the priors) affects the results one obtains after fitting the model. I have made sure that my units are in km.
```
nu <- 1 # Matern smoothness parameter
alpha <- 2
r0 <- 0.5
#Matern SPDE model object using inla.pcmatern
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
                            alpha = alpha,
                            constr = TRUE,
                            prior.range = c(1, 0.01), # P(range < 1) = .01
                            prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01) # P(sigma > 5) = .01
                            )
```
Also, I would like to know if there's any rule of thumb when setting the priors for the precision of the random noise term

```
hyper.prec = list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(5, 0.01)))
```

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Setting the priors for the SPDE
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Setting the priors for the SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brian,

We certainly can help you on how to set a specific prior. However, please consider that prior distributions on a model are to formally add the personal (or expert) prior knowledge on that. Therefore I cannot set a prior distribution for your problem because I do not have a prior knowledge about it.

On how to set a prior. For example, if you want to use the PC-priors (in the inla.spde2.pcmater() model builder function) you can play with the two probability statements. The paper for this is in this link https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01621459.2017.1415907

For the (practical) range parameter, you use P(range < reference) = a. Some use it to set a low probability (small a) for a small range (small reference). Some use median.

For the marginal standard deviation (sigma) the probability statement is P(sigma > reference) = a. Some use median and some use a (relatively) big reference along with a small probability.

In summary, if we both were to solve the same problem, we may use different prior and therefore the posterior will differ. When the information from the data dominates, the difference from the prior is negligible on the posterior.

I hope this helps,
Elias

messages.body_plain:
>From the methodological aspect, I recommend starting with
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211675322000057
and then to consider the references therein.

For applications, there is a tutorial-book. From the (https://www.r-inla.org/) you click in LearnMore, then in Books and you will see the book link along with links for the gitbook version and the code to reproduce the examples. However, please remember that it used an old (around 6 years old now) inla version. The recent ones improved a lot. All the examples there can be updated with modern inla however mostly all of them still work. Several examples were along the line of using the SPDE models as a model component in more complex models and still serve as inspiration.

The main recent developments in terms of applications of SPDE models are with the inlabru package (https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlabru) and you can find practical tutorials within the "Articles" section. Also, consider the rSPDE (https://github.com/davidbolin/rSPDE/) which deals with the estimation of the smoothness parameter as well.

best regards,
Elias

Hi INLA team,

I am working on a spatial model with point and grid data for soil moisture, which includes 20 points and 100 grids. Here is my model:

Here is the main part of the code:

the projection matrix for the grid data:

Aa <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = locin, block = block, block.rescale = "sum")

  formula <- Y ~ 0 + alpha_1 + alpha_2 + alpha_3 + x +
    f(u_1_0, y_1_0, model = 'iid',
      hyper = list(prec = list( initial = 15,fixed = TRUE))) +
    f(u_2_0, y_2_0, model = 'iid',
      hyper = list(prec = list( initial = 15,fixed = TRUE))) +
    f(u_1, model=spde, extraconstr = list(A=matrix(1,ncol=mesh$n,nrow=1), e=matrix(0,ncol=1))) +
    f(u_2, model=spde, extraconstr = list(A=matrix(1,ncol=mesh$n,nrow=1), e=matrix(0,ncol=1))) +
    f(u_3, model=spde, extraconstr = list(A=matrix(1,ncol=mesh$n,nrow=1), e=matrix(0,ncol=1))) +
    f(y_2, copy="u_2_0", fixed=FALSE, hyper=list(beta=list(prior = 'normal', param = c(0, 10))))+
    f(y_1, copy="u_1_0", fixed=FALSE, hyper=list(beta=list(prior = 'normal', param = c(0, 10))))

  res1 <- inla(formula, family = c("gaussian","gaussian",'gaussian','gaussian','gaussian'),
               data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE,A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)),
               verbose =TRUE,
               control.inla = list(linear.correction = TRUE, strategy = "adaptive", int.strategy = "eb"),
               control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, control.gcpo=list(enable=TRUE), cpo = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config=TRUE),
               control.family = list(hfix, pprec,hfix, pprec, pprec))

I keep getting this error and on the some occasions it does run, it takes about three hours to complete. :
Mode not sufficient accurate; switch to a stupid local search strategy. maxld= 282858.887 fn=1467 theta= 18.444 -2.557 18.444 -1.347 2.899 7.612 -8.591 7.621 -8.594 0.747 0.237 -0.022 -0.022 [3.1, 1.79] GMRFLib_opt_estimate_hessian: ensure spd for Hessian: mode seems fine
Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 740, Thread: 2 Failed to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

Can anyone help me with this issue?  Thanks for your help :)

Best wishes
Weiyue

that, then move to this dynamics, when Sigma = diagonal matrix, and then when
its general.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Finn everything you wrote was really useful.

On Tuesday, June 4, 2024 at 1:56:11 AM UTC-5 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Theta1 and theta2 are the internal parameterisation of the “humanly interpretable” parameter. The spde2.result function converts them into humanly interpretable format. But when using pcmatern models, already the $summary.hyperpar output is in humanly interpretable scale (range and sigma).
>
> However, when I said spatial variability I meant just that, and _not_ the model _parameter_ sigma. The distinction is subtle, and if one had a iid model component they would be almost the same as each other. But in the presence of strong spatial correlation, the actual variability within the domain can be _smaller_ than the model parameter value.
> I’m referring to the difference between
>   Var(u(s)|Y) = sigma^2,
> which  is the posterior  variance of the random field u(.), and
>   V(D) = \frac{1}{|D|} \int_D [u(s) - M(D)]^2 ds,
> where
>   M(D) = \frac{1}{|D|} \int u(s) ds
>
> The posterior expectation of V(D) is the “posterior expected mean square deviation from the spatial average”, and this is more directly measuring the amount of spatial variability in u(s) than \sigma^2.
>
> That said, people tend to ignore that and just talk about sigma anyway…
>
> “Statistical insignificance” of a variable is usually not a reason to remove it from the model; I would only remove it if keeping it in the model causes numerical problems or excessive runtime. But this is a large complicated philosophical issue that one can spend weeks on in a modern class on statistical modelling…
>
> Finn
>
> > On 3 Jun 2024, at 22:34, Richard <richard...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿Just to add something about Theta1 and Theta2, I see that theta1 is negative so I guess is not the range of the SPDE but then I am not sure what does theta1 and theta 2 mean:
> >
> > mod.field = inla.spde2.result(res, name="s", spde)
> > mod.field$summary.hyperpar
> >
> >
> >
> > On Monday, June 3, 2024 at 3:02:19 PM UTC-5 Richard wrote:
> > > Hi Finn, thank you for your answer. I read the paper you mentioned and I think that I get what you mentioned.
> > > Reading the paper in some part you did this
> > >
> > >
> > > So I gues that I should do what you mentioned, run the model the first time with the spatial effect and see which ones do not have the 0 in the posterior credible interval and then a second time without the spatial effect and see which ones have the 0 and see how in the presence of f(s, model = spde) some variables can or cannot explain the spatial effect?
> > >
> > > And to compute the overall spatial variability I think that with INLA one can do that using this:
> > >
> > > mod.field = inla.spde2.result(res, name="s", spde)
> > > mod.field$summary.hyperpar
> > >
> > > So I get theta1 and theta2 and their mean, sd, an posterior credible interval, then if theta2 (I guess that is sigma and theta1 is the range) is significant their mean would be the overall spatial variability?
> > >
> > > And lastly, one question that appeared while reading this, I can use the significance of the variables to see how this changes with and without spatial effect as mentioned above, but even if the variable is non significant that is not enough reason to remove the variable, even in the presence of a spatial effect, right? I am asking this because I did a model selection using the DIC criteria but when I see the significance to see how much of the spatial effect is explained by them, one of my two covariables are not significant so that covariable cannot explain the log-spatial effect (I have a lognormal model) but the predictions are better with this term (and I am mostly interested only on those predictions), but in the paper you mentioned, because of that significance you are going to remove the variables, so what should be the correct procedure here?
> > >
> > > Thank you!!
> > >
> > > On Monday, June 3, 2024 at 9:01:09 AM UTC-5 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > this question has multiple potential answers, depending on the reason
> > > > for asking it, and no one true correct answer. For instance, since the
> > > > spatial field component has posterior correlation with the "fixed
> > > > effects", the variation contribution of each individual effect can add
> > > > up to more than the combined variability, so computing a "percentage
> > > > of explained variance" doesn't necessarily mean what one thinks it
> > > > means.
> > > >
> > > > But you may be on the right track in thinking about what happens to
> > > > the model when removing one model components, and comparing the
> > > > results. We did something along those lines in
> > > > Yuan Yuan, Fabian E. Bachl, Finn Lindgren, David L. Borchers, Janine
> > > > B. Illian, Stephen T. Buckland, Håvard Rue, and Tim Gerrodette (2017),
> > > > "Point process models for spatio-temporal distance sampling data from
> > > > a large-scale survey of blue whales", Annals of Applied Statistics,
> > > > 11, 2270--2297, doi:10.1214/17-AOAS1078
> > > > There, we compared the spatial model predictions with and without the
> > > > random field component present in the estimation, and computed the
> > > > overall spatial variability (in the spatial context, overall spatial
> > > > variability is arguably the relevant quantity, and not raw statistical
> > > > variance at the observation locations).
> > > > What you describe sounds similar, but with looking only at the
> > > > locations where you have observations.
> > > > Both versions require you to run the model twice; one with the f(s,
> > > > ...) component, and once without it. There's no special magic to
> > > > this.
> > > >
> > > > Note:
> > > > Due to the posterior dependence, I prefer looking at the combined
> > > > component effects when comparing models; i.e. I would mainly compare
> > > > combined predictor values, and not the individual component estimates,
> > > > as those have different interpretation in the presence of other model
> > > > components (spatial confounding is virtually ubiquitous, and one
> > > > should not expect "spatial fixed effect" estimates to remain unchanged
> > > > when adding other spatial components to the model).
> > > >
> > > > Finn
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, 3 Jun 2024 at 03:26, Richard <richard...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.subject: inla.hyperpar.sample
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

Would someone kindly explain to me what the function inla.hyperpar.sample does? I know it samples from the approximate joint posterior distribution of hyperparameters, but how is it approximated? And is this joint distribution conditional on the data and the latent field?

I can also provide more information on my research question to give an example, but for now I am more interested in theory and trying to better understand what I am actually assuming when I use the inla.hyperpar.sample function.
I have not found any documentation on this function, but please send it to me if you have any.

Thanks in advance for your help!
Kind regards,
Chiara

> On another note, again even for a very coarse prediction grid (dim (20,20)), predict() takes really long (~hour), could it be that since the mesh is much more fine than the prediction grid, something goes wrong with the interpolation?
>
> Στις Πέμπτη 6 Ιουνίου 2024 στις 10:36:24 π.μ. UTC+2, ο χρήστης kyriakos nikolaou έγραψε:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Thank you, I changed such that all the polygons and points are sf and the the covariate fields as terra, and I also made sure to pad them  so no need for evaluating missing values. with this changes predict()  finishes running  without any errors, and the result seems reasonable.
> >
> > However it is still quite slow. For example with  n.samples = 10 it still took about 2 hours (with the fit being only 30 min)  this might be related to my mesh being to dense (number of elements is 31068). Moreover even if I try to predict only the effect of spatial covariates, without the random effect, it still takes quite some time.
> >
> > I would also like to ask some more questions around predict and how it can be used on new realizations.
> >
> > 1) From what I understand, in regards to the lgcp model, predict() samples from the marginal posterior distributions created by inla to sort of give an expected posterior (given that the field is a random hidden structure). is that correct? (therefore that's why it also takes so long even when I look at only covariate effects, as it tries to marginalize the random effect)
> >
> > 2) how does the evaluation of predict compare with the evaluations that inla gets on the mesh nodes? should they be similar for fine enough mesh? I guess it can be used to interpolate/predict in places where there is no node but does this makes sense to do that for a really fine mesh?
> >
> > 3) And last, given the problem that I am dealing with, that i want to study multiple realizations. I would like to use the fitted model (the posteriors of its parameters/hyperparameters) to predict the mean density of points of a new realization without points (not in the fitting set) given the covariate fields . My guess is that the best I can do is use the medians for the parameters of the covariates and not consider the random effect. In this case my prediction can be thought of as the mean density BUT with a missing random variation (quantified by a certain rho and sigma) that we cannot know since its isotropic.
> >
> > Thanks again
> > Kyriacos
> >
> > Στις Τρίτη 4 Ιουνίου 2024 στις 2:18:54 μ.μ. UTC+2, ο χρήστης Finn Lindgren έγραψε:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > having the covariate evaluator function call fill_missing() is the likely issue with runtime for predictions, in case that means it tries to evaluate it for all those locations outside the grid. But 40x40 should be ok even for that.
> > > But to be safe, you might need to make the covariate field complete before calling the inlabru methods, so it only needs to do that _once_, and not every time you evaluate the predictor.
> > > But with just 1 sample and 40x40 I wouldn't expect it to take that long.
> > >
> > > Can you consider changing from sp to sf? I'm reluctant to spend time on debugging sp specific code anymore; if sf/terra works, it would be better.
> > > (Most of the online inlabru examples have been converted to sf/terra, although we don't seem to have a good example for how to do fill_missing in combination with terra rasters; the principle is the same as for sp, but the code details are slightly different I think).
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > On Tue, 4 Jun 2024 at 13:58, kyriakos nikolaou <kyria...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hello,
> > > >
> > > > In regards to the last questions, here are my package versions
> > > > inlabru 2.10.1
> > > > INLA 23.09.09
> > > > fmesher 0.1.5
> > > >
> > > > moreover in the end i settled for a single intercept.
> > > >
> > > > However I want to double check whether what I get makes sense. the fitting seems to work but the prediction takes way too long. fitting takes 30 min, prediction even with 1 trial seems to be taking indefinitely 1 day running and still
> > > >
> > > > So, my current setting is the following: I stitched together my realization domains, and then constructed bounding boxes for the outer mesh. The final result is the following: you can see the mesh, domain (in red, which i have a spatial polygons data frame called all.polygons.spdf), points (in green) looks like this

> > > >

> > > >
> > > >
> > > >

> > > >   v <- eval_spatial(celldata$covariates$spdf$distance$bn_distance, where)
> > > >   if (any(is.na <http://is.na>(v))) {

> > > >
> > > > # construct model

> > > >   DBN(eval.DBN(.data.), model = "linear") +
> > > >   IM(eval.IM(.data.), model = "linear") +
> > > >   IE(eval.IE(.data.), model = "linear") +
> > > >   Intercept(1)
> > > >
> > > > # fit

> > > >
> > > > pred.df <- fm_pixels(mesh, dims = c(40, 40), mask = SpatialPolygons(list(cells_polygons[[3]])), minimal = FALSE,format = "sp")
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > intensity.full <- predict(fit, pred.df, ~ exp(  field +
> > > >                                               DBN +
> > > >                                               IM +
> > > >                                               IE +
> > > >                                               Intercept), n.samples = 1)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > on another note,
> > > > fm_int(list(coordinates = mesh),all.polygons.spdf)
> > > > seems to be working properly
> > > >
> > > > Any clue on what might be going wrong with the prediction time to be seemingly endless?
> > > >
> > > > thank you for your support,
> > > > Kyriacos  Nicolaou

Okay. I get that it's parameterizing the precision matrix with a band format, but I'm at a loss as to how exactly to do that.

For the precision matrix, I get that the diagonals and positions off the diagonals up to distance 2 will be non-zero, but it's not clear to me exactly what I put there. Following the ar1 example in the vignette, would substituting rho with gamma*T be accurate (or at least a step in the right direction; see attached photo)? I'm not sure how I'd add the d_(t-1) part. Is there a way to easily insert the observation equation simultaneously (eq. 6 in the Jonsen et al. paper)?

Apologies if these are very basic questions for you. It's admittedly been several years since I've done anything related to matrix algebra.

Kind regards,
Nick

On Wednesday, June 5, 2024 at 7:13:16 PM UTC+9:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
>
> You have 4 hyperparameter, the correlation, two variances and the angle.
>
> given these, then eq~2 gives the dynamics for the location. note the implicite
> singularity as 'd' is two locations, but the current location at time t, is the
> previous location at time t-1.
>
> this dynamics gives a block diagonal precision matrix which you have to add in
> rgeneric.
>
> I would suggest to start with a simpler example, like a simple RW1 and code
> that, then move to this dynamics, when Sigma = diagonal matrix, and then when
> its general.
>
>
>
> On Mon, 2024-06-03 at 09:40 -0700, Nick Freymueller wrote:
> > Thanks for your recommendations, Håvard.
> >
> > I've gotten some of the way through what a DCRW model would look like given
> > the vignette you sent, the GMRF book, and the online gitbook. However, there
> > are a few points for what I'd specify for the inla.rgeneric.define model that
> > I'm still a bit confused on. I'm not sure how to specify the bivariate nature
> > of mu or how to specify the auto-regressive parts of this. Additionally, I'm
> > not sure exactly what I'd specify for the precision matrix and normalizing
> > constants. I get where the non-zero elements in the precision matrix are
> > supposed to be given the structure of the model, but I'm lost as to how
> > exactly to populate these non-zero elements.
> >
> > I've attached what I have been working on so far. Any and all
> > help/suggestions/recommendations would be much appreciated. I'd eventually
> > like to get to a place where I can specify the data similar to that shown here
> > with specified error terms where available
> > (https://ianjonsen.github.io/aniMotum/articles/Overview.html#light-level-geolo
> > cation-data) and run multiple individuals that are indexed hierarchically.
> >
> > Kind regards,

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

In an attempt to trace the problem in slow predict times, I scanned over the number of realizations I fit the model on and the time it takes to fit lgcp()) and predict(fit,n.samples = 1)

This should not be surprising as fit and predict is now done on a larger mesh (number of elements scales with number of realization)

However if you look at the fraction of these times, for some reason the prediction time raises faster when we go from one to two disjoint regions

And last, it seems that the time for prediction is intendent of what is predicted, I also tried on very coarse grids (dim (40,40)) and the time it takes seems to be the same.

The above seem to make some sense if we consider that the sampling of predict samples also random fields from the other realizations to predict on new realizations. However the random fields on other realizations cannot contribute as being "interpolated" to another realization. Therefore there is a lot of effort sampling for nothing.

What do you think?

Kyriacos

messages.subject: change reference temperature
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA team,

I am working on an INLA model to understand the effect of temperature on mortality, where the behaviour of temperature is captured by natural cubic splines with 4 basis functions without intercept. I understand that this can be modelled by a random walk of order 2, but for this example I will like to work with natural splines.

My model basically looks like:
form_eg <- deaths ~ 1 +
  offset(log(population)) +
  factor(dow) +
  Temp_matrix +  # temperature
  f(id_doy, model = "rw2", scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE, hyper = hyper_rw2) +
  f(id_year, model = "iid", constr = TRUE, hyper = hyper_iid)

where Temp_matrix is specified by
knots <- quantile(sampleData$temperature_lag03,c(10,75,90)/100, na.rm=T)
Temp_matrix <- ns(sampleData$temperature_lag03, knots = knots, intercept = FALSE)

I have used the following code to plot the result:
coeff_inlaEg <- inla_eg$summary.fixed[8:11,]
ns_median <- Temp_matrix  %*% coeff_inlaEg[c(paste0(1:4)),"0.5quant"]
ns_LL <- Temp_matrix  %*% coeff_inlaEg[c(paste0(1:4)),"0.025quant"]
ns_UL <- Temp_matrix %*% coeff_inlaEg[c(paste0(1:4)),"0.975quant"]

The result is as follows, but what we find awkward is that by default the reference levels is the minimum temperature. Is there a simple way to change the reference category to say 10oC? We are happy to define this either in the inla call or when making predictions.

Thank you in advance.
Best,
Xinyi

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I want to implement a Restricted Spatial Regression (RSR) model with InlaBru. The model would be as follows: Y(s)=β⋅X(s)+ü(s)+ϵ(s) with :

- Y(s) as the response variable
- X(s) as my variable of interest
- ü(s) a spatial random effect, which would be the projection of the  spatial effect u(s) that follows a Matèrn with a specific range and  precision: ü(s) = (Id - X %% (Xt %% X)^(-1) %% Xt)*u(s)
- ϵ(s) a white noise

For this, I applied the following command in Inlabru:

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Implementation of an RSR model with Inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
your second approach doesn't work as written, since weights is only
allowed to be a vector. One could in principle attach the matrix
multiplication to the component mapper pipeline, bu an easier option
in your case would be to apply the matrix operation in the predictor
expression instead:

model_RSR3 <-   bru(~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde),
  formula = Y ~ X + as.vector((Id - X %*% (Xt %*% X)^(-1) %*% Xt) %*% u),

  family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)

or, numerically/memory-wise much better,

model_RSR3 <-   bru(~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde),
  formula = Y ~ X + u - X * sum(X * u) / sum(X^2),

  family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)

Note that if you want to use the predict() function, you then have to
compute the appropriate matrix operation for that as well, in order to
get to your ü variable.
Projections that depend on the observed locations have some
theoretically nice properties, but are quite painful to work with in
practice, when you want to evaluate the model more generally.
One potential problem is that I think the Jacobian of that expression
is a dense matrix, so I would expect estimation to be slow and use _a
lot_ of memory.

If needed, you can access the latent variables for the spde basis
coefficients, with u_latent. That way, you could choose to apply an
integration constraint instead of a sum over the observed locations.
But it all depends on _why_ you want the particular model. Presumably
some type of anti-confounding approach? Removing the entirety of x
from u is then not necessarily a good thing. But most importantly,
interpreting the results needs to be done with some care, as the
projection part will be an integral part of the model. The dense
matrix problem mentioned above is also likely to make the estimation
impractical. A alternative may be to just estimate the unconstrained
model, and then reparameterise it afterwards, in the predict call:

predict(..., ~ {
  scale <- sum(X * u) / sum(X^2)
  X_new <- X + X * scale
  u_new <- u - X * scale
  list(X_new, u_new)
})

(with some needed modifications if prediction is done at new locations
etc, as mentioned above)

The end result isn't exactly the same thing as the model you asked
for, but probably just as valid.

Note: did specifying control.predictor=list(A = ...) give you a
warning? If not, I should add that, as inlabru will always override
that setting with its own matrices, as an integral part of the
algorithm.

Finn

messages.subject: Anisotropy possibility in R-INLA SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-inla group,

I am checking to see if there have been any updates on setting anisotropy in INLA-SPDE. I inquired with your team a few years ago, and there were no such settings available at that time. There are some packages inspired by R-INLA, but based on the TMB approach, that include an anisotropy option. Typically, these packages add a rotation matrix, H, to the range parameter. In my opinion, it is similar to the Barrier model within the INLA framework (when I say "similar", I mean they both adjust the range parameter, but of course, differently).

I saw a post from Finn last year mentioning that your team is working on a better approach to address the anisotropy issue. I would like to get the most recent updates on this.

Thanks,
Rujia

                        LL = ns_LL,

I'm finding a way, perhaps similar to this approach in the FAQ <https://www.r-inla.org/faq#h.pb4g1pwbmtli>, to do the as the title.

More specifically, let say we have

y1 = time + X, time = {1, 2, 3, 4}

I'd like the second likelihood of the form

y2 =  (time_3 - time_2) + X

y2 does not exist in any other times than the time_3

Does that make sense and is there a way to code this for a two likelihood model?

Thanks,
Kinh

messages.subject: some results using a spatio-temporal model with gaussian data
messages.subject_clean: some results using a spatio-temporal model with gaussian data
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I am creating a spatio-temporal model for variable following a gaussian distribution, the best model was created using :

### preparing the INLA data frame with O, E, 3 ids
S <- length(unique(final_data$County))
T <- length(unique(final_data$YEAR))

t.from <- min(final_data$YEAR)
t.to <http://t.to> <- max(final_data$YEAR)

Data <- final_data[order(final_data$YEAR,final_data$County),]

Data.INLA <- data.frame(O = Data$Corn_Yield,
                        E = Data[, c("Temp","precipitation","Hum","dlh","wind","DNI")],
                        ID.area = rep(1:S,T),
                        ID.year = rep(1:T,each=S),
                        ID.area.year = seq(1,T*S))

### Neighboring structure
g <- inla.read.graph("iowa.graph")

Q.xi <- matrix(0, g$n, g$n)
for (i in 1:g$n){
  Q.xi[i,i]=g$nnbs[[i]]
  Q.xi[i,g$nbs[[i]]]=-1
}

Q.Leroux <- diag(S)-Q.xi

### temporal structure matrix
D1 <- diff(diag(T),differences=1)
Q.gammaRW1 <- t(D1)%*%D1

D2 <- diff(diag(T),differences=2)
Q.gammaRW2 <- t(D2)%*%D2

sdunif="expression:
  logdens=-log_precision/2;
  return(logdens)"

lunif = "expression:
    a = 1;
    b = 1;
    beta = exp(theta)/(1+exp(theta));
    logdens = lgamma(a+b)-lgamma(a)-lgamma(b)+(a-1)*log(beta)+(b-1)*log(1-beta);
    log_jacobian = log(beta*(1-beta));
    return(logdens+log_jacobian)"

### posterior patterns distribution
compute.patterns <- TRUE

if(compute.patterns){
  source("posterior_lincombs.R")
}else{
  all.lc <http://all.lc> <- NULL
}

strategy <- "simplified.laplace"

## The model

R <- kronecker(Q.gammaRW1,Q.xi)
r.def <- S+T-1
A1 <- kronecker(matrix(1,1,T),diag(S))
A2 <- kronecker(diag(T),matrix(1,1,S))
A.constr <- rbind(A1[-1,],A2[-1,])

f.TypeIV.RW1_2 <- O ~ E.precipitation+E.Temp+E.Hum+E.dlh+E.wind+E.DNI+f(ID.area, model="generic1", Cmatrix=Q.Leroux, constr=TRUE,hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif),beta=list(prior=lunif))) +
  f(ID.year, model="rw1", constr=TRUE,
    hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif))) +
  f(ID.area.year, model="generic0", Cmatrix=R, rankdef=r.def,
    constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif)),
    extraconstr=list(A=A.constr, e=rep(0,S+T-2)))

TypeIV.RW1_2 <- inla(f.TypeIV.RW1_2, family="gaussian", data=Data.INLA,
                   control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, cdf=c(log(1))),
                   control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE),
                   lincomb=all.lc <http://all.lc>
                   ,control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.01)))),
                   control.inla=list(strategy=strategy))

I am struggling now to follow up, when i want to create maps for spatial risk, should I use exponential transformations ? or should I keep the same scale ?

# exponential transformation
spatial.risk <- unlist(lapply(Model$marginals.lincomb.derived[2:(S+1)], function(x) inla.emarginal(function(x) exp(x), x)))

# same scale
spatial.risk <- unlist(lapply(Model$marginals.lincomb.derived[2:(S+1)], function(x) inla.emarginal(function(x) x, x)))

same questions for all the other analysis I should cary on ?

Thanks,
Ayoub.

messages.body_plain:
Dear respected members of the INLA community,

I have been trying to use the BAPC/INLA package to project age-standardized rates. Below is the code I am using:

if(requireNamespace("INLA", quietly = TRUE)) {
    require(INLA)
    data(FemLCSweden)
    data(FemPYSweden)
    data(whostandard)

    lc_sweden <- APCList(FemLCSweden, FemPYSweden, gf=5)

    result  <- BAPC(lc_sweden, predict=list(npredict=10, retro=TRUE),
        verbose=FALSE, stdweight=whostandard[6:17,2])

    plotBAPC(result, scale=10^5, type="ageSpecProj", showdata=TRUE)

    ## Assume the data for 2000 to 2010 are not observed
    ## (projection results are the same as above)
    FemLCSweden[51:60,] <- NA

    lc_sweden <- APCList(FemLCSweden, FemPYSweden, gf=5)

    result  <- BAPC(lc_sweden, predict=list(npredict=10, retro=FALSE),
        verbose=FALSE, stdweight=whostandard[6:17,2])

    plotBAPC(result, scale=10^5, type="ageSpecProj", showdata=TRUE)
}

However, I keep encountering the error: Error in seq.default(xmin, xmax, length.out = n) : 'from' must be a finite number.

I have tried multiple attempts to troubleshoot this issue, but it persists. Could you please guide how to resolve this error?

Best regards,
Enyu

Y1 = 1 + 1.1 * t + rnorm(N) # outcome 1
Y2 = 0.5 + 2.0 * (Y1[t==3] - Y1[t==2]) + rnorm(n) # outcome 2

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Apologies if this has already been asked - a quick search through the forum didn't turn up anything.

I'm getting the following error when I fit an intercept-only model and am wondering if it's because my model syntax is bogus, or there's an issue with some package version (matrix package maybe)?

Error: non-conformable matrix dimensions in .diag2T.smart(e1, e2, kind = "d") - e2

Here is code to reproduce the error:

library(INLA)
library(inlabru)

# Simulate data
dat <- data.frame(y = rbinom(100,1,0.1))

# Analysis
comps <- ~ Intercept(1)

present_like <- like(
  family = "binomial",
  data = dat,
  formula = as.formula('y ~ Intercept')
)

fit <- bru(
  comps,
  present_like,
  options = list(bru_verbose = 4,
                 bru_debug = TRUE)
)

Note that if I add an additional covariate effect, the model will fit without an error:

library(INLA)
library(inlabru)

# Simulate data
dat <- data.frame(y = rbinom(100,1,0.1),
                  x = rnorm(100))

# Analysis
comps <- ~ Intercept(1) + x_effect(x)

present_like <- like(
  family = "binomial",
  data = dat,
  formula = y ~ Intercept + x_effect
)

fit <- bru(
  comps,
  present_like,
  options = list(bru_verbose = 4)
)

messages.subject: Doubt about inla.group.cv() crashing INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I am interested in looking for some metric of the performance of the spatial model when doing predictions so in another answer I got recommended this paper:

  Automatic cross-validation in structured models: Is it time to leave out leave-one-out?

And I also read
LEAVE-GROUP-OUT CROSS-VALIDATION FOR LATENT GAUSSIAN MODELS

And I am trying to do that in my spatial model with the SPDE approach but I am facing some issues:

I have some model, let´s say res, I want to use the LGOCV so I would have:

m <- 3

r <- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(res, num.level.sets = m)

But every time I get

Error: The inla program call crashed.

Does anyone know how to solve this? I am able to do the LOOCV without problem and then get the logarithmic score

r <- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(res)
-mean(log(r$cv[1:number of observations]))

But because this is a spatial model I know this not the best option but even using other data I am getting the same problem.

Here I add an example with a dataset of R

library(geoR)
library(ggplot2)
library(INLA)

ggplot(data.frame(cbind(parana$coords, Rainfall = parana$data)))+
    geom_point(aes(east, north, color = Rainfall), size = 2) +
    coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
    scale_color_gradient(low = "blue", high = "orange") +
    geom_path(data = data.frame(parana$border), aes(east, north)) +
    theme_bw()

coo <- parana$coords
summary(dist(coo))

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  loc = coo, offset = c(50, 100),
  cutoff = 1, max.edge = c(30, 60)
)
plot(mesh)
points(coo, col = "red")

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE)

indexs <- inla.spde.make.index("s", spde$n.spde)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coo)

bb <- bbox(parana$border)
x <- seq(bb[1, "min"] - 1, bb[1, "max"] + 1, length.out = 50)
y <- seq(bb[2, "min"] - 1, bb[2, "max"] + 1, length.out = 50)
coop <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))

ind <- point.in.polygon(
  coop[, 1], coop[, 2],
  parana$border[, 1], parana$border[, 2]
)
coop <- coop[which(ind == 1), ]
plot(coop, asp = 1)

Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coop)

stk.e <- inla.stack(
  tag = "est",
  data = list(y = parana$data),
  A = list(1, A),
  effects = list(data.frame(b0 = rep(1, nrow(coo))), s = indexs)
)

# stack for prediction stk.p
stk.p <- inla.stack(
  tag = "pred",
  data = list(y = NA),
  A = list(1, Ap),
  effects = list(data.frame(b0 = rep(1, nrow(coop))), s = indexs)
)

# stk.full has stk.e and stk.p
stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.e, stk.p)

formula <- y ~ 0 + b0 + f(s, model = spde)

res <- inla(formula,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
  control.predictor = list(
    compute = TRUE,
    A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)
  )
)

r <- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(res, num.level.sets = 1)

And here is where it crash

Le mercredi 12 juin 2024 à 16:01:51 UTC+2, jérémy Lamouroux a écrit :
> Thank you for your response. I will try what you explain.
> No, specifying control.predictor = list(A = ...) did not give me a warning.
>
> Best regards,
> Jérémy
> Le mercredi 12 juin 2024 à 12:48:25 UTC+2, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
> > Hi,
> > your second approach doesn't work as written, since weights is only
> > allowed to be a vector. One could in principle attach the matrix
> > multiplication to the component mapper pipeline, bu an easier option
> > in your case would be to apply the matrix operation in the predictor
> > expression instead:
> >
> > model_RSR3 <- bru(~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde),
> > formula = Y ~ X + as.vector((Id - X %*% (Xt %*% X)^(-1) %*% Xt) %*% u),
> > family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)
> >
> > or, numerically/memory-wise much better,
> >
> > model_RSR3 <- bru(~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde),
> > formula = Y ~ X + u - X * sum(X * u) / sum(X^2),
> > family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)
> >
> > Note that if you want to use the predict() function, you then have to
> > compute the appropriate matrix operation for that as well, in order to
> > get to your ü variable.
> > Projections that depend on the observed locations have some
> > theoretically nice properties, but are quite painful to work with in
> > practice, when you want to evaluate the model more generally.
> > One potential problem is that I think the Jacobian of that expression
> > is a dense matrix, so I would expect estimation to be slow and use _a
> > lot_ of memory.
> >
> > If needed, you can access the latent variables for the spde basis
> > coefficients, with u_latent. That way, you could choose to apply an
> > integration constraint instead of a sum over the observed locations.
> > But it all depends on _why_ you want the particular model. Presumably
> > some type of anti-confounding approach? Removing the entirety of x
> > from u is then not necessarily a good thing. But most importantly,
> > interpreting the results needs to be done with some care, as the
> > projection part will be an integral part of the model. The dense
> > matrix problem mentioned above is also likely to make the estimation
> > impractical. A alternative may be to just estimate the unconstrained
> > model, and then reparameterise it afterwards, in the predict call:
> >
> > predict(..., ~ {
> > scale <- sum(X * u) / sum(X^2)
> > X_new <- X + X * scale
> > u_new <- u - X * scale
> > list(X_new, u_new)
> > })
> >
> > (with some needed modifications if prediction is done at new locations
> > etc, as mentioned above)
> >
> > The end result isn't exactly the same thing as the model you asked
> > for, but probably just as valid.
> >
> > Note: did specifying control.predictor=list(A = ...) give you a
> > warning? If not, I should add that, as inlabru will always override
> > that setting with its own matrices, as an integral part of the
> > algorithm.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On Wed, 12 Jun 2024 at 10:11, jérémy Lamouroux
> > <jeremyla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > I want to implement a Restricted Spatial Regression (RSR) model with InlaBru. The model would be as follows: Y(s)=β⋅X(s)+ü(s)+ϵ(s) with :
> > >
> > > - Y(s) as the response variable
> > > - X(s) as my variable of interest
> > > - ü(s) a spatial random effect, which would be the projection of the spatial effect u(s) that follows a Matèrn with a specific range and precision: ü(s) = (Id - X %% (Xt %% X)^(-1) %% Xt)*u(s)
> > > - ϵ(s) a white noise
> > >
> > > For this, I applied the following command in Inlabru:
> > >
> > > model_RSR <- bru(Y ~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde), family = "gaussian", data = df_sf, options = list(control.predictor=list(A = df_sf$x)))
> > >
> > > I thought that the control.predictor would allow me to make the scalar product ⟨X,u⟩=0, which would make X and u orthogonal and thus would allow applying an RSR model via Inlabru.
> > >
> > > Another method I was thinking of was to apply this projection in the "weights" of the spatial effect, that is:
> > >

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Implementation of an RSR model with Inlabru
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Implementation of an RSR model with Inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Don't include -1 in the like() formula; like() interprets it as a
general R expression, so -1 literally subtracts 1. Only the component
specification interprets -1 in the "don't include an intercept" way.
(Better to use 0+ instead of -1, to avoid accidental mistakes like
that).

The sum() expression is more efficient than the full matrix version.
However, in your original question, X was a single column, which my
rewriting took advantage of. In your latest query, it's no longer
clear to me if X is a single vector, or a multi-column matrix.
I'm guessing the error is due to overflow in the predictor expression
calculations. This will happen if X has large values.

To get a similarly more efficient version when X has multiple columns
you want to orthogonalise against, you need to rewrite it differently.
The key is to avoid constructing X %*% t(X), which is a large dense
matrix, when all you need it the "skinny" matrix X %*% (t(X) %*% u).
To do it in matrix form, therefore simply include parenthesis in the
required places, to make sure you never construct a large dense
matrix, and use solve(A, b) instead of inverting a matrix.
Unfortunately, if you do this in the like() expression, a large dense
matrix will be created internally anyway, since the Jacobian of the
expression will involve the matrix X %*% t(X). This is the case even
if X only has a single column.

Therefore, I strongly suggest not estimating the model like this, and
instead only adjust for orthogonality in the posterior
samples/predictions (like one of my suggestions indicated).  Unless
the aim is _specifically_ to analyse the estimation behaviour of
applying the constraint in the estimation, but then you'll need to
spend time getting an understanding of all the numerical and
computational problems inherent in that approach.

Best wishes,
Finn

On Wed, 19 Jun 2024 at 09:32, jérémy Lamouroux

<jeremyla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello, thanks again for your previous answer.
>
> With the same model but using X*=(1_n, X), after computing to find a numerical formula, we implement it like the following: where 1n is a column of ones representing the intercept, and X is defined as previously.
>
>
> res_RSR_with_i <- bru( components = ~-1+ intercept(1) + X_Effect(X) + u(geometry, model = spde), like( formula = Y ~ -1 + intercept + X_Effect + u - (sum(u) * sum(X^2) + X * (length(X) * sum(X * u) - sum(u) * sum(X)) - sum(X * u) * sum(X)) / (length(X) * sum(X^2) - sum(X)^2), family = "gaussian", data = df_sf ), options = list( control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = FALSE), control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"), verbose = FALSE ) )
>
>
> Is there another way to do it, using matrix form ?

>
> It runs well, but we have 2 types of warning messages that seem to repeat for several iterations:
>
>
> Warnings in bru_compute_linearisation.component(model[["effects"]][[label]], : Non-finite (-Inf/Inf/NaN) entries detected in predictor 'u' plus eps. Warnings in bru_compute_linearisation.component(model[["effects"]][[label]], : Non-finite (-Inf/Inf/NaN) entries detected in predictor derivatives for 'u'; treated as 0.0.
>
>
> What can cause this type of warning in our formula?

> Thank you for your help,
> Best Regards,
> Jérémy
> Le mercredi 12 juin 2024 à 16:01:51 UTC+2, jérémy Lamouroux a écrit :
>>

>>

>> Jérémy
>> Le mercredi 12 juin 2024 à 12:48:25 UTC+2, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
>>>
>>> Hi,
>>> your second approach doesn't work as written, since weights is only
>>> allowed to be a vector. One could in principle attach the matrix
>>> multiplication to the component mapper pipeline, bu an easier option
>>> in your case would be to apply the matrix operation in the predictor
>>> expression instead:
>>>
>>> model_RSR3 <- bru(~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde),
>>> formula = Y ~ X + as.vector((Id - X %*% (Xt %*% X)^(-1) %*% Xt) %*% u),
>>> family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)
>>>
>>> or, numerically/memory-wise much better,
>>>
>>> model_RSR3 <- bru(~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde),
>>> formula = Y ~ X + u - X * sum(X * u) / sum(X^2),
>>> family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)
>>>
>>> Note that if you want to use the predict() function, you then have to
>>> compute the appropriate matrix operation for that as well, in order to
>>> get to your ü variable.
>>> Projections that depend on the observed locations have some
>>> theoretically nice properties, but are quite painful to work with in
>>> practice, when you want to evaluate the model more generally.
>>> One potential problem is that I think the Jacobian of that expression
>>> is a dense matrix, so I would expect estimation to be slow and use _a
>>> lot_ of memory.
>>>
>>> If needed, you can access the latent variables for the spde basis
>>> coefficients, with u_latent. That way, you could choose to apply an
>>> integration constraint instead of a sum over the observed locations.
>>> But it all depends on _why_ you want the particular model. Presumably
>>> some type of anti-confounding approach? Removing the entirety of x
>>> from u is then not necessarily a good thing. But most importantly,
>>> interpreting the results needs to be done with some care, as the
>>> projection part will be an integral part of the model. The dense
>>> matrix problem mentioned above is also likely to make the estimation
>>> impractical. A alternative may be to just estimate the unconstrained
>>> model, and then reparameterise it afterwards, in the predict call:
>>>
>>> predict(..., ~ {
>>> scale <- sum(X * u) / sum(X^2)
>>> X_new <- X + X * scale
>>> u_new <- u - X * scale
>>> list(X_new, u_new)
>>> })
>>>
>>> (with some needed modifications if prediction is done at new locations
>>> etc, as mentioned above)
>>>
>>> The end result isn't exactly the same thing as the model you asked
>>> for, but probably just as valid.
>>>
>>> Note: did specifying control.predictor=list(A = ...) give you a
>>> warning? If not, I should add that, as inlabru will always override
>>> that setting with its own matrices, as an integral part of the
>>> algorithm.
>>>
>>> Finn
>>>
>>> On Wed, 12 Jun 2024 at 10:11, jérémy Lamouroux

>>> > - ü(s) a spatial random effect, which would be the projection of the spatial effect u(s) that follows a Matèrn with a specific range and precision: ü(s) = (Id - X %% (Xt %% X)^(-1) %% Xt)*u(s)
>>> > - ϵ(s) a white noise

>>> > For this, I applied the following command in Inlabru:
>>> >
>>> > model_RSR <- bru(Y ~ -1 + X + u(geometry, model = spde), family = "gaussian", data = df_sf, options = list(control.predictor=list(A = df_sf$x)))
>>> >

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] 3D spatio-temproal modelling
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yes, it's possible, but I'm not aware of any full examples.

For the 3D part, one option is to use the spde model constructions
from the experimental https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlamesh3d
package (provide a tetrahedralization of space, and it does the rest,
like inla.spde2.matern).
This can then be used as part of a separable space-time model, using
the "group" feature, e.g.
 + f(space, model=spde_3d, group = time, control.group=list(model="ar1"))
This is the method that requires the least new coding on your part.

Another alternative is to construct the spatial part as a rgeneric or
cgeneric model, and then proceed in the same way.

A third option is to implement the whole space-time model as an
rgeneric or cgeneric model.

Finn

Subject: Re: [r-inla] 3D spatio-temproal modelling

Hi,

Yes, it's possible, but I'm not aware of any full examples.

For the 3D part, one option is to use the spde model constructions
from the experimental https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlamesh3d
package (provide a tetrahedralization of space, and it does the rest,
like inla.spde2.matern).
This can then be used as part of a separable space-time model, using
the "group" feature, e.g.
 + f(space, model=spde_3d, group = time, control.group=list(model="ar1"))
This is the method that requires the least new coding on your part.

Another alternative is to construct the spatial part as a rgeneric or
cgeneric model, and then proceed in the same way.

A third option is to implement the whole space-time model as an
rgeneric or cgeneric model.

Finn

messages.subject: Rankdef-argument: interpretation and usage
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

How should the rankdef-argument be properly used with generic0 models?

For instance, let us say we consider a temporal RW2 model + an intercept term. How should rankdef then be defined in the following settings:

(1) We set the intercept to zero. No constraints needed.
(2) We add a sum to zero constraint on the latent RW2 field.
(3) We add an additional trend term, so that we need both constraints on the rw2-term.

Is the randef independent of the number of constraints?
What happens internally in INLA with this argument?

Best

Fredrik

messages.subject: Saving warning messages
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone! I'm conducting a simulation study adjusting BYM models to different simulated datasets. In some scenarios, the model fits, but warning messages like these are generated:

*** warning *** max_correction = 25.01 >= 25.00, 'vb.correction' is aborted *** You can change the emergency value (current value=25.00) by *** 'control.inla=list(control.vb=list(emergency=...))' *** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc. *** warning *** delta[0] is NAN, 'vb.correction' is aborted *** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc."

I would like to save these messages to identify in which simulation they occurred, but I'm having trouble doing so. Please help me!

besag.iid.fun <- function(result) {
    ady <- inla.read.graph(filename = "map.adj")
    train_df <- dplyr::bind_cols(
        data.frame(result$codigo_comuna),
        x1masE = result$x1masE,
        x2masE = result$x2masE,
        E = result$E,
        y = result$y,
        real.RR = result$real.RR,
        re_u = result$re_u,
        re_v = result$re_v
    )

    # Lista para almacenar warnings
    warnings_list <- list()

    # Función para manejar advertencias
    warning_handler <- function(w) {
        warnings_list[[length(warnings_list) + 1]] <<- conditionMessage(w)
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }

    # Ejecutar inla con tryCatch para capturar advertencias
    resultadobym <- tryCatch({
        withCallingHandlers(
            inla(
                formula = y ~ x1masE + x2masE +
                    f(re_u, model = "besag", graph = ady, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE) +
                    f(re_v, model = "iid"),
                family = "poisson",
                data = train_df,
                E = E,
                control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, dic = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
                control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)
            ),
            warning = warning_handler
        )
    }, error = function(e) e)

    # Verificar si hubo un error
    if (inherits(resultadobym, "error")) {
        return(list(
            error = "Se produjo un error al ejecutar inla."
        ))
    }

    # Extracción de resultados
    efectos.fijos <- resultadobym$summary.fixed
    waic <- resultadobym$waic$waic
    dic <- resultadobym$dic$dic
    cpo <- resultadobym$cpo$cpo
    precision_u <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar$mean[1]
    precision_v <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar$mean[2]
    RR.ajustada.post <http://RR.ajustada.post> <- resultadobym$summary.fitted.values[,"mean"]
    LL.ajustada.post <http://LL.ajustada.post> <- resultadobym$summary.fitted.values[, "0.025quant"]
    UL.ajustada.post <http://UL.ajustada.post> <- resultadobym$summary.fitted.values[, "0.975quant"]
    sd_precision_u <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[1,2]
    q1.precision_u <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[1,3]
    q0.5precision_u <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[1,4]
    q3precision_u <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[1,5]
    sd_precision_v <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[2,2]
    q1.precision_v <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[2,3]
    q0.5precision_v <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[2,4]
    q3precision_v <- resultadobym$summary.hyperpar[2,5]
    x1masE <- result$x1masE
    x2masE <- result$x2masE

    # Determinar el mensaje de warning
    warning_message <- if (length(warnings_list) > 0) {
        paste(warnings_list, collapse = "; ")
    } else {
        "OK"
    }

    return(list(
        efectos.fijos = efectos.fijos,
        waic = waic,
        dic = dic,
        cpo = cpo,
        x1masE = x1masE,
        x2masE = x2masE,
        precision_u = precision_u,
        precision_v = precision_v,
        real.RR = result$real.RR,
        RR.ajustada.post <http://RR.ajustada.post> = RR.ajustada.post <http://RR.ajustada.post>,
        UL.ajustada.post <http://UL.ajustada.post> = UL.ajustada.post <http://UL.ajustada.post>,
        LL.ajustada.post <http://LL.ajustada.post> = LL.ajustada.post <http://LL.ajustada.post>,
        sd_precision_u = sd_precision_u,
        q1.precision_u = q1.precision_u,
        q0.5precision_u = q0.5precision_u,
        q3precision_u = q3precision_u,
        sd_precision_v = sd_precision_v,
        q1.precision_v = q1.precision_v,
        q0.5precision_v = q0.5precision_v,
        q3precision_v = q3precision_v,
        warnings = warning_message  # Agregar el mensaje de warning
    ))
}
Thank you!!

Dear INLA community

I am trying to get samples of the observed data using the posterior found with INLA but I am not sure if I am doing correclty.
I know about the functions inla.posterior.sample() and inla.posterior.sample.eval(), I am using right now inla.posterior.sample() as I see that in the part "latent" there are the APredictor so if the observed data was of length n, I take the first n predictors, is that correct? And as long as I understand inla.posterior.sample.eval() is only for sampling the posterior predictive.

I see that something similar is done when getting the predictions of the model and the reason why I take the approach mentioned above. As seen in this part of the code we are only taking the index.pred observations when trying to get the predictions:

But if we are trying to get the index of the fitted values it would be:

index.est <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, "est")$data
res$summary.fitted.values[index.est, "mean"] #for the estimations

So if I want to get samples of the fitted values to sample the observed data I do

sim <- inla.posterior.sample(500, res) #In this object in the part of latent I would get the #first n predictors for an observed data of size n, just like for the case of the fitted #values

sim[[1]]$latent[1:n] #where n is the size of the observed data

Is this approach correct to getting samples of the observed data?

The answer to your final question is “no”, since it produces samples of the predictor values, which are typically the expectation values for the observation model, _not_ ‘observations’ in themselves. Some.g. In a y ~ Poisson(lambda) model, the predictor (with link function applied) gives you lambda values, and to get y values you’d need to call rpois() afterwards. This would make sense for the “pred” part. (And the “est” part, in some cases).

messages.subject: Different precision for random walk setting in inlabru
messages.subject_clean: Different precision for random walk setting in inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Dear discusssion community,

I am constructing a smooth function based on random walk model and spatial effect with inlabru.

My model have four variables, x, y, z, k; and I want to fit a model of y as response variable and x with second order random effect, z with 1d spatial spde random effect. The following is my code:

cmp <- y ~ fz(z, model = z.spde) + fx(x, model = "rw2")

model <- bru(components=cmp, family = "gaussian", data=data, options=list(control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-10)))

>From data visualization, I notice that y highly fluctuates when k is low, so I want to set a smaller precision for the prior of the rw2 latent effect when k is less than a threshold value and a larger precision when k is greater than this threshold.

I wonder whether and how this can be achieved in inlabru function?

Many thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Different precision for random walk setting in inlabru
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Different precision for random walk setting in inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

this is not inlabru specific, but rather applies to how to achieve
that with any inla model.

How to do it depends a bit on _how_ you would like k to affect the
model, e.g. if it's enough to have a different variance of the driving
noise for the rw2 model depending on if k is above a given value or
not, or if you want a continuous dependence on k.
It also depends on if you specifically require a rw2 model, or if some
other similar model would be ok.
But in all those cases, the easiest option I'm aware of is likely to
write your own rgeneric implementation of the model you want to have,
where you have full freedom in how k should influence the precision
matrix. You can see what the general rw2 model for irregular locations
is defined as in the Lindgren and Rue paper from 2008
(https://www.jstor.org/stable/41000297). Simpler options are to scale
the marginal distribution in a way that depends o k, but that's not
the same thing as changing the internal variability parameter of the
rw2 model, so you need to think more carefully about precisely what
model you want to have.
Finn

messages.subject: Simulating spatial effect in samples of the observed data
messages.subject_clean: Simulating spatial effect in samples of the observed data
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

In a last post I asked about how to get samples of the observed data, which I was interested in get to do a posterior predictive check, with the help of Dr Finn Lindgren I was able to get those simulated predictions doing the following:

parameters_sampled <- inla.posterior.sample(500, res)

#example for one sample
sample <- rnorm(138, parameters_sampled[[1]]$latent[1:138], 1/sqrt(parameters_sampled[[1]]$hyperpar[1]))

That would get me a sample of what the model thinks observed data could look like.

But in my case I have an SPDE so I assume that I not only need the sample I got using rnorm but also add the spatial random effect, here is where I am having trouble.

I know that the spatial random effect has a distribution Multivariate Gaussian with mean zero and precision matrix, so I need to have the posterior of that precision matrix to get samples of the posterior predictive distribution.

I knwo that for samples of the predictions when trying to add an spatial effect to those samples one would usually do something like this:

Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(
    mesh = mesh,
    loc = cbind(pred.data$x, pred.data$y)
)

fun2 <- function()
    return(
        iIntercept +
        x1 * pred.data$x1 +
        Ap %*% s
     )

But that needs to use inla.posterior.sample.eval which does not work for samples of the observed data but I read something similar here for the observed data: https://groups.google.com/u/1/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/VGmWQ31887I?pli=1

So I adapted the code for what I needed

d <- as.data.frame(coordenadas_muestras)
coo <- cbind(d$X, d$Y)

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE)
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coo) #coo are the coordinates of the samples

parameters_sampled <- inla.posterior.sample(500, res) #res is the inla() model which #says log(y)~normal

for (i in 1:500){
  Q = inla.spde.precision(spde, theta=c(parameters_sampled[[i]]$hyperpar[2], parameters_sampled[[i]]$hyperpar[3]))
  omega_s = inla.qsample(n=1, Q = Q)
  omega_s = omega_s[ ,1]
  omega_s = drop(A %*% omega_s)

  sigma_e <- 0.5

  lin.pred <- rnorm(138, parameters_sampled[[i]]$latent[1:138], 1/sqrt(parameters_sampled[[i]]$hyperpar[1])) +
    omega_s

  y[,i] <- lin.pred + sigma_e*rnorm(138) #here the person had that 0.5 but I am not sure why

}

Now I have a matrix where each column is a sample of what the model could think the observed data could look like.

Is this the right way to simulate the spatial random effect in INLA?

messages.body_plain:
n <- 30
y <- rpois(n, exp(2))
idx <- 1:n
for (emerg in c(0.001,  25)) {
    cat("emergency = ", emerg, "\n")
    r <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx, vb.correct = T, initial = log(1), fixed = T),
              data = data.frame(y, idx),
              control.inla = list(control.vb = list(emergency = emerg),
                                  int.strategy = "eb"),
              family = "poisson")
    if (length(grep("max_correction = ", r$logfile)) > 0) {
        cat("VB ABORTED\n")
    } else {
        cat("VB OK\n")

    }
}

messages.subject: Accounting for relative area sampled
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am trying to model temporal trends in different geographical regions using a random walk. A simplified verison of my model looks like this:

y ~ intercept + region + rw(year)

Where y is observed density of a species in a small area within the region.
I have a different number of observations of y between regions and years and regions have different sizes, meaning that one observation in region A might mean 1% of the area was sampled, but one observation in region B might mean 2%of the area was sampled.

In a frequentist approach I would probably use weights to account for these differences, but that does not seem correct in a Bayesian approach (at least from what I've gathered reading this forum).

Do you have any recommendation on how to deal with this or could you point me to further reading material?

Thank you very much,

Paula

messages.subject: Factors in Hurdle Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA group,

I am attempting to fit a Hurdle Poisson model in INLA and have run into an issue with the factors defined. I have been following the Likelihood for hurdle model thread <https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/DPvHIGcbd0E> to define a model using the bioChemist data from the pscl package <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/pscl/versions/1.5.9/topics/bioChemists>. I have attached reproducible code to help explain the problem but the issue seems to be with the term 'z.fem' in the model.

z.fem should be a factor of Men and Women with the reference being 'Men'. So when I fit the model, I am expecting to see only 'z.femWomen' in the fixed effects. However I am seeing both 'z.femMen' and 'z.femWomen'. These two fixed effects , along with the 'z.intercept' term, have extremely large credible intervals as well which made me realised there could be an issue. However, I have no idea how to fix the issue. As part of the Hurdle model, I defined the same fixed effects for the count part of the model (prefixed with 'y.'). For 'y.fem' there is not the same issue.

If anyone was able to offer some advice that would be great!

Thanks !!
Connor

messages.subject_clean: [DLM with INLA] Location are too close for ...
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
This message is provided for the information of other users.
I use INLA to do DLM on time series which can be long term. Recently, when processing a 35-year series on a weekly basis, I got the following message:
*** inla.core.safe:  The inla program failed, but will rerun in case better initial values may help. tr
y=1/1
Erreur dans inla.core.safe(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts,  :
  Locations are too close for f(i, model="rw2", ...):  min(diff(sort(x)))/diff(range(x)) = 5.528e-04 < 1
e-03
  You can fix this by some kind of binning, see ?inla.group
  If you want/need to bypass this check at your own risk, do
        > m = get("inla.models", inla.get.inlaEnv())
        > m$latent$rw2$min.diff = NULL
        > assign("inla.models", m, inla.get.inlaEnv())
The inla program failed and the maximum number of tries has been reached.
The time series has 1810 weeks, and :
> loc <- c(1:1810)
> min(diff(sort(loc)))/diff(range(loc))
[1] 0.0005527916
Thus, the error is induced by the large number of weeks in the time series, i.e. by the long-term nature of the series. I therefore decided to ignore the test, as indicated by the error message, and the results were correct.

Thank you for the helpdesk team's work.
DS

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Accounting for relative area sampled
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Accounting for relative area sampled
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paula,

the inlabru code itself looks fine. As to how to account for variable
sampling efforts, you should first think about that problem outside
the scope of how to implement it; otherwise you risk locking yourself
into "solutions" that exist in code, but aren't necessarily suitable
to the actual problem you're solving. That said, taking your suggested
code, your model effectively is

y^A_i ~ Gamma(mean = exp(eta_i), prec = prec_A)
y^B_j ~ Gamma(mean = exp(eta_j), prec = prec_B)

where each eta_i is the linear predictor value at location i.

This says that you're allowing the variance of the individual
measurements to have a different variance in regions A and B.
This is different from accounting for how much sampling you're doing
in each region, _unless_ you only have a single observation in each
region; it's not entirely clear from your initial post. If you only
have a single observation in each region, then the multi-gamma model
above won't work, as there won't be any information about prec_A and
prec_B from those single observations.
If each sampling area is of the same size, then the model above
inherently handles sampling effort, via how many observations you
have.
But if there are multiple sampling areas of different size, you could
figure out what the resulting observation model _should_ be, under
some reasonable assumption.
For Poisson count observations, one simply has that y_i ~
Possion(Area_i * exp(eta_i)) (if eta is smooth enough that a single
representative value in each sampling area is sufficient).
But for continuous non-Gaussian measurements it's less obvious if
there's a "correct" model. But perhaps you can use it as inspiration.

Finn

On Wed, 26 Jun 2024 at 15:36, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Paula,
>
> the inlabru code itself looks fine. As to how to account for variable
> sampling efforts, you should first think about that problem outside
> the scope of how to implement it; otherwise you risk locking yourself
> into "solutions" that exist in code, but aren't necessarily suitable
> to the actual problem you're solving. That said, taking your suggested
> code, your model effectively is
>
> y^A_i ~ Gamma(mean = exp(eta_i), prec = prec_A)
> y^B_j ~ Gamma(mean = exp(eta_j), prec = prec_B)
>
> where each eta_i is the linear predictor value at location i.
>
> This says that you're allowing the variance of the individual
> measurements to have a different variance in regions A and B.
> This is different from accounting for how much sampling you're doing
> in each region, _unless_ you only have a single observation in each
> region; it's not entirely clear from your initial post. If you only
> have a single observation in each region, then the multi-gamma model
> above won't work, as there won't be any information about prec_A and
> prec_B from those single observations.
> If each sampling area is of the same size, then the model above
> inherently handles sampling effort, via how many observations you
> have.
> But if there are multiple sampling areas of different size, you could
> figure out what the resulting observation model _should_ be, under
> some reasonable assumption.
> For Poisson count observations, one simply has that y_i ~
> Possion(Area_i * exp(eta_i)) (if eta is smooth enough that a single
> representative value in each sampling area is sufficient).
> But for continuous non-Gaussian measurements it's less obvious if
> there's a "correct" model. But perhaps you can use it as inspiration.
>
> Finn
